5        3.   PHONE BOXES.

20        4.   BARRAZA V. CRICKET WIRELESS, LLC.                           
21        In a prior action against defendant regarding false advertising, an order of ours denied 
22    defendant’s motion to compel arbitration under California and Missouri law.  Barraza v. 
23    Cricket Wireless, LLC, No. C 15-02471 WHA, 2015 WL 6689396, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 3, 
24    2015).  The order stated that defendant’s Quick Start Guide “lacked any indication of its 
25    contractual nature.”  Id. at *5 (emphasis in original).  The plaintiffs’ failure to opt out did not 
26    constitute acceptance because a reasonable consumer would not have been aware of the 
27    arbitration provision buried inside the Quick Start Guide.  Moreover, the plaintiffs “had no 
1    And defendant’s use of the phrase “terms and conditions” rather than “contract” on boxes and 
2    receipts was not consequential.  The order held that a summary trial was necessary to resolve a 
3    credibility issue of whether the plaintiffs had actually read the materials notifying them of the 
4    in-the-box terms.                                                    
5        This order follows full briefing and a telephonic hearing.       
6                               ANALYSIS                                  
7        1.   RULING ON DEFENDANT’S MOTION IS PROPER.                     
8        Defendant argues that Schwarzchild v. Tse, 69 F.3d 293 (9th Cir. 1995), proposed that, 
9    prior to provision of class notice and the expiration of the opt-out deadline, an order 
10    compelling arbitration does not bind absent class members (Br. 1 n. 1).  This order finds that it 
11    may exclude from the class definition absent class members who are likely subject to 
12    arbitration, but those excluded persons will still be free to bring suit later and litigate 
13    arbitrability issues individually.  Thus, ruling on the motion to compel arbitration will help fine 
14    tune the class.                                                      
15        2.   CHOICE-OF-LAW.                                              
16        “The choice-of-law inquiry has two levels.  First, we must determine whose choice-of-
17    law rules govern.  Second, applying those rules, we determine whose law applies.”  
18    Schoenberg v. Exportadora de Sal, S.A. de C.V., 930 F.2d 777, 782 (9th Cir. 1991).   
19        Here, the choice-of-law rules of the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws (1969) 
20    govern because there is federal question jurisdiction in this RICO action.  Ibid.  There is no 
21    California statute on choice-of-law.  See Paulsen v. CNF Inc., 559 F.3d 1061, 1080 (9th Cir. 
22    2009).  So the Restatement requires that this order analyze the factors in Section 6, as follows:  
23    the interstate system requires this order to apply the proper state substantive law to each class 
24    member to avoid abridging or enlarging rights under 28 U.S.C. Section 2072(b); California law 
25    on in-the-box contracts differs from that of other interested states; the law on in-the-box 
26    contracts is not so complex as to prevent application of different states’ laws; and general 
27    contract law will provide some uniformity of result.  Thus, this order shall apply the laws of 
1    the respective class members’ states of residence at the time of purchase.  And the prior class 
2    certification order justifies the parties’ expectation that this order do so.   
3        3.   VALIDITY OF THE ARBITRATION PROVISIONS.                     
4        The Federal Arbitration Act states that arbitration agreements “shall be valid, irrevocable, 
5    and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any 
6    contract.”  9 U.S.C. § 2.  “A party seeking to compel arbitration has the burden under the FAA 
7    to show (1) the existence of a valid, written agreement to arbitrate; and, if it exists, (2) that the 
8    agreement to arbitrate encompasses the dispute at issue.”  Ashbey v. Archstone Prop. Mgmt., 
9    Inc., 785 F.3d 1320, 1323 (9th Cir. 2015).                           
10        In determining the former, “federal courts ‘apply ordinary state-law principles that 
11    govern the formation of contracts.’”  Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, Inc., 763 F.3d 1171, 1175 
12    (9th Cir. 2014) (citation omitted).  In determining the latter, “any doubts concerning the scope 
13    of arbitrable issues should be resolved in favor of arbitration . . . .”  Moses H. Cone Mem’l 
14    Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 24–25 (1983).  If both questions are answered in 
15    the affirmative, then the FAA requires enforcement of the arbitration agreement according to 
16    its terms, “leav[ing] no place for the exercise of discretion by a district court.”  Dean Witter 
17    Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U.S. 213, 218 (1985).  But “[g]enerally applicable contract 
18    defenses, such as fraud, duress, or unconscionability, may be applied to invalidate arbitration 
19    agreements without contravening [FAA] § 2.”  Dr.’s Ass’n, Inc. v. Casarotto, 517 U.S. 681, 
20    682 (1996).                                                          
21             A.   DEFENDANT’S ADVERTISEMENTS DID NOT DEFEAT CONTRACT     
                   FORMATION.                                             
22                                                                         
         Plaintiffs argue that, due to defendant’s “no contract” advertisements, class members did 
23                                                                         
     not believe that they were entering into contractual relationships with defendant (Opp. 5).  So 
24                                                                         
     class members could not have assented to the terms accompanying their phones (see ibid.).   
25                                                                         
         But Barraza stated the following:                                
26                                                                         
              “No Contract” in the context of advertisements for          
27             telecommunications services is meant to distinguish services with 
              “No Contract” ads to trick consumers into unknowingly assenting 
1             to arbitration, rather than to convey [defendant]'s offer of service 
              without an annual commitment.  Defendant[] cannot now be    
2             precluded from enforcing contracts against plaintiffs . . . . 
3    2015 WL 6689396, at *6.  Other courts have agreed with this conclusion.  E.g., Jialu Wu v. 
4    iTalk Glob. Commc’ns, Inc., No. CV 20-7150 PSG (PJWx), 2020 WL 8461696, at *3 (C.D. 
5    Cal. Oct. 21, 2020) (Judge Philip S. Gutierrez).  One of defendant’s employees also stated here 
6    that defendant’s “no contract” policy referred only to the time commitment for defendant’s 
7    services (Dkt. No. 177-17, Towster Dep. 250).  Thus, the “no contract” policy alone did not 
8    defeat contract formation, and it did not invalidate the arbitration provisions.   
9             B.   THE QUICK START GUIDE WOULD LIKELY REQUIRE ARBITRATION IN 
                   STATES THAT FOLLOW SEVENTH CIRCUIT DECISIONS.          
10                                                                         
         There are two Seventh Circuit decisions that enforce in-the-box contracts, and several 
11                                                                         
     states follow them.  In ProCD, Inc. v. Zeidenberg, the plaintiff sold an encoded CD-ROM disc 
12                                                                         
     inside a box.  86 F.3d 1447, 1450 (7th Cir. 1996).  The outside of the box warned of an 
13                                                                         
     enclosed license, which also appeared on the computer screen before the CD-ROM disc could 
14                                                                         
     be used.  Ibid.  The license expressly provided the plaintiffs an opportunity to return the disc if 
15                                                                         
     they found the terms unsatisfactory.  Id. at 1453.                   
16                                                                         
         Under Wisconsin law, ProCD enforced the license because “[the defendant] extended an 
17                                                                         
     opportunity to reject if a buyer should find the license terms unsatisfactory; [the plaintiff] 
18                                                                         
     inspected the package, tried out the software, learned of the license, and did not reject the 
19                                                                         
     goods.”  Id. at 1452–53.  It emphasized that, regarding transactions for consumer goods, 
20                                                                         
     “[n]otice on the outside, terms on the inside, and a right to return the software for a refund if 
21                                                                         
     the terms are unacceptable (a right that the license expressly extends), may be a means of doing 
22                                                                         
     business valuable to buyers and sellers alike.”  Id. at 1451.  ProCD rejected the conclusion that 
23                                                                         
     general contract terms must be conspicuous to be enforceable.  Id. at 1453.   
24                                                                         
         In a later Seventh Circuit case, Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc., 105 F.3d 1147, 1148 (7th Cir. 
25                                                                         
     1997), the plaintiffs ordered and paid for a computer over the phone.  The computer and a list 
26                                                                         
     of terms were enclosed in a box that the defendant sent to the plaintiffs.  Ibid.  The outside of 
27                                                                         
     the box, however, did not display a notice that additional terms were enclosed.  Id. at 1150.  
1    The terms stated that they would govern disputes between the parties unless the plaintiffs 
2    returned the computer within thirty days.  Id. at 1149.  The plaintiffs did not return the 
3    computer within thirty days.  Ibid.  The court followed ProCD and held that, under both 
4    Illinois and South Dakota law, the plaintiffs accepted the offer “by keeping the computer 
5    beyond thirty days.”  Id. at 1150.                                   
6        Here, the Quick Start Guide, but not the Terms and Conditions booklet, would likely 
7    require arbitration of class members’ claims in states that follow ProCD and Hill.  As to the 
8    Quick Start Guide, it is enforceable as an in-the-box contract.  Like in ProCD and Hill, in 
9    which the terms inside the product boxes expressly provided an opportunity to opt out of 
10    arbitration or to return the products, here, the Quick Start Guide inside defendant’s phone 
11    boxes expressly provided an opportunity to opt out of the arbitration provision (Dkt. No. 199-
12    2).  Although the Quick Start Guide was not obviously contractual, and the arbitration 
13    provision was inconspicuous (ibid.), ultimately an arbitration provision need not be 
14    conspicuous to be enforceable under ProCD.  86 F.3d at 1453.  Notably, because Barraza 
15    applied California and Missouri law — which require conspicuous terms — enforcing the 
16    Quick Start Guide here does not conflict with Barraza.               
17        Thus, all class members who made a purchase prior to May 18, 2014 and who, at the time 
18    of such purchase, resided in states that follow ProCD and Hill would likely be subject to 
19    arbitration, except for those who opted out of arbitration (which could be up to 1,099 persons) 
20    (Dkt. No. 199-9, ¶ 10).  These states follow ProCD and Hill:         
21             •  Delaware.  Westendorf v. Gateway 2000, Inc., No. 16913, 2000 WL 307369, 
22               at *2–3 (Del. Ch. Mar. 16, 2000); Rinaldi v. Iomega Corp., No. 98C-09-064-
23               RRC, 1999 WL 1442014, at *3–4 (Del. Super. Ct. Sept. 3, 1999). 
24             •  Florida.  Salco Distributors, LLC v. iCode, Inc., No. 8:05-CV-642-T-
25               27TGW, 2006 WL 449156, at *2 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 22, 2006) (Judge James 
26               Whittemore); see Dye v. Tamko Bldg. Prods., Inc., 908 F.3d 675, 682–84 
27               (11th Cir. 2018); Chamberlain v. LG Electronics U.S.A., Inc., No. CV 17-
1               2046-MWF (PLAx), 2017 WL 3084270, at *4 (C.D. Cal. June 29, 2017) 
2               (Judge Michael W. Fitzgerald).                            
3             •  Illinois.  Hill, 105 F.3d at 1149.                       
4             •  Indiana.  Sprint Sols., Inc. v. Aldridge, 50 F. Supp. 3d 1024, 1026 (S.D. Ind. 
5               2014) (Judge Tanya Walton Pratt).                         
6             •  Louisiana.  O’Quin v. Verizon Wireless, 256 F. Supp. 2d 512, 516 (M.D. La. 
7               2003) (Judge James Brady).                                
8             •  Maine.  Stenzel v. Dell Inc., No. Civ.A. CV-03-323, 2004 WL 1433657, at *3 
9               (Me. Super. Ct. Mar. 11, 2004).                           
10             •  Maryland.  See Sprint Nextel Corp. v. Simple Cell Inc., 31 F. Supp. 3d 710, 
11               712–13 (D. Md. 2014) (Judge Catherine C. Blake).          
12             •  New York.  Brower v. Gateway 2000, Inc., 676 N.Y.S.2d 569, 572 (N.Y. 
13               App. Div. 1998); see Chamberlain, 2017 WL 3084270, at *3. 
14             •  Rhode Island.  Defontes v. Dell, Inc., 984 A.2d 1061, 1071 (R.I. 2009). 
15             •  South Dakota.  Hill, 105 F.3d at 1149.                   
16             •  Tennessee.  MDB, LLC v. BellSouth Advert. & Pub. Corp., No. 3:07-CV-126, 
17               2007 WL 2782287, at *3–4 (E.D. Tenn. Sept. 21, 2007) (Judge Thomas W. 
18               Phillips).                                                
19             •  Washington.  M.A. Mortenson Co., Inc. v. Timberline Software Corp., 140 
20               Wash. 2d 568, 583–84 (2000); see Chamberlain, 2017 WL 3084270, at *4. 
21             •  West Virginia.  Schultz v. AT & T Wireless Services, Inc., 376 F. Supp. 2d 
22               685, 691–92 (N.D. W. Va. 2005) (Judge Frederick P. Stamp Jr.). 
23             •  Wisconsin.  ProCD, 86 F.3d at 1450–51.                   
24        By contrast, the Terms and Conditions booklet is not enforceable because, unlike the 
25    contracts in ProCD and Hill, it did not expressly extend a right to reject the terms.  It contained 
26    neither a return provision nor an opt-out clause.  Defendant counterargues that its online 
27    policies were incorporated into the Terms and Conditions booklet, and those online policies 
1    contained a seven-day return provision (Reply Br. 11).  But the failure to expressly state the 
2    provision in the booklet rendered it insufficient to provide an opportunity to reject the terms.   
3        Moreover, the Terms and Conditions booklet stated that opening the phone box, 
4    activating the service, or starting an application constitutes acceptance, conflicting with the 
5    online provision that failure to return a phone within seven days constitutes acceptance (Dkt. 
6    No. 199-5).  Thus, because the booklet stated that its terms control over conflicting outside 
7    terms, the return provision on defendant’s website could not save it.   
8        Additionally, even if the return policy did control, opening a phone box would not have 
9    constituted acceptance because class members could not have reviewed the terms prior to 
10    acceptance, as required under ProCD and Hill.  Further, defendant’s argument that class 
11    members ratified the booklet terms is meritless because ratification would not change the fact 
12    that there was never a meaningful opportunity to reject the terms.   
13             C.   CLASS MEMBERS NEED NOT ARBITRATE UNDER CALIFORNIA LAW. 
14        In California, “[a] party who is bound by a contract is bound by all its terms, whether or 
15    not the party was aware of them.”  Norcia v. Samsung Telecomms. Am., LLC, 845 F.3d 1279, 
16    1284 (9th Cir. 2017).  This is true even when the party did not read the contract.  Ibid. 
17        “[T]he essential elements for a contract are (1) ‘[p]arties capable of contracting;’ (2) 
18    ‘[t]heir consent;’ (3) ‘[a] lawful object;’ and (4) ‘[s]ufficient cause or consideration.’”  United 
19    States ex rel. Oliver v. Parsons Co., 195 F.3d 457, 462 (9th Cir. 1999) (quoting Cal. Civ. Code 
20    § 1550).  “‘Mutual assent may be manifested by written or spoken words, or by conduct’ . . . .”  
21    Knutson v. Sirius XM Radio Inc., 771 F.3d 559, 565 (9th Cir. 2014) (citation omitted).  “Courts 
22    must determine whether the outward manifestations of consent would lead a reasonable person 
23    to believe the offeree has assented . . . .”  Ibid.                  
24        Regarding acceptance, our court of appeals has stated the following: 

25             As a general rule, “silence or inaction does not constitute 
              acceptance of an offer.” California courts have long held that “[a]n 
26             offer made to another, either orally or in writing, cannot be turned 
              into an agreement because the person to whom it is made or sent 
27             makes no reply, even though the offer states that silence will be 
1    Norcia, 845 F.3d at 1284 (citations omitted).  “There are exceptions to this rule, however.  An 
2    offeree's silence may be deemed to be consent to a contract when the offeree has a duty to 
3    respond to an offer and fails to act in the face of this duty.”  Id. at 1284–85.  “An offeree's 
4    silence may also be treated as consent to a contract when the party retains the benefit offered.”  
5    Id. at 1285.                                                         
6        But, “[e]ven if there is an applicable exception to the general rule that silence does not 
7    constitute acceptance, courts have rejected the argument that an offeree's silence constitutes 
8    consent to a contract when the offeree reasonably did not know that an offer had been made.”  
9    Ibid.  “An offeree, regardless of apparent manifestation of his consent, is not bound by 
10    inconspicuous contractual provisions of which he was unaware, contained in a document 
11    whose contractual nature is not obvious.”  Windsor Mills, Inc. v. Collins & Aikman Corp., 25 
12    Cal.App.3d 987, 993 (1972).                                          
13        Finally, California does not follow ProCD or Hill with respect to in-the-box contracts.  
14    Norcia, 845 F.3d at 1289.                                            
15        Here, the California class members did not assent to the terms of the Quick Start Guide 
16    or the Terms and Conditions booklet, so they need not arbitrate under California law.  
17    Moreover, defendant has not shown that any class members manifested an intent to use silence 
18    or failure to opt out as assent, such as by signing either of the pamphlets.  Although defendant 
19    provided each class member with a receipt that referred to an agreement to arbitrate, defendant 
20    does not state that any class members signed such receipts or read them (Moses Decl., ¶ 7, 
21    Exh. A).  Thus, the class members’ silence did not equal acceptance.  Further, defendant does 
22    not argue that the class members had a duty to respond or retained any benefit by failing to act.  
23    Finally, the pamphlets cannot be enforced as in-the-box contracts under California law.   
24        Defendant argues that the class members had “a wide array of notice” regarding the 
25    arbitration provisions (Br. 24).  But defendant misunderstands Norcia.  Norcia turned on assent 
26    — not notice.  See Norcia, 845 F.3d at 1285–86.  Even if the class members here were on 
27    notice of the arbitration provisions, there is no indication that they manifested assent to them. 
1        Further, although some of defendant’s phone boxes stated that purchase, activation, or 
2    use of the phones constituted agreement to the arbitration provision (Keser Decl., ¶ 6), Norcia 
3    did not hold that such notice creates a contract.  See Norcia, 845 F.3d at 1286–87.  Moreover, 
4    the references here to the terms were in fine print on the sides or the backs of the phone boxes.
